requirements.where: Discussion; The Most Ethical Path; Recommendation

technical_issues.issue: Volkswagen case misrepresented: text says electric vehicles and crash-safety tests; the actual scandal concerned diesel emissions cheating.
Reference [3] lacks a URL and reference [4] is malformed; referencing is not consistently Harvard or IEEE.
Accepting the contract while delaying launches and concluding Not Ship is inconsistent; no conditions for permissible shipping are specified.
Apple reference does not clearly support the claimed competitive advantage over Samsung and Google.
The 1 percent failure calculation is hypothetical and not presented as evidence-based risk data.
No abstract of approximately 150 words is included.
Large-scale testing to inform future safety improvements is not explicitly evaluated.
The chip contract company is listed as a stakeholder but its interests are not discussed.

overall: Clear structure and a justified do-not-ship conclusion, but missing abstract, limited and partly inaccurate references, weak stakeholder/trade-off analysis, and no conditions for shipping. Marks reflect good argument but only moderate research and format.

feedback.summary: You built a clear, well-structured report with a justified Not Ship conclusion and a useful for/against discussion. The main gaps are the missing abstract, limited and partly inaccurate referencing, underdeveloped stakeholder trade-offs, and no conditions for permissible shipping. Your marks are unchanged; the feedback below shows how to move each criterion to the next level.
next_steps: Add a ~150-word abstract and at least one relevant visual element (e.g., a stakeholder impact table or risk matrix); proofread and format all references consistently in Harvard or IEEE.

Correct and expand your evidence: reframe the Volkswagen case as diesel emissions cheating, complete reference [3] with a URL, fix reference [4], replace the hypothetical 1% failure figure with sourced risk data, and make the Apple reference directly support your competitive-advantage claim.

Strengthen stakeholder and trade-off analysis: discuss the chip contract company’s interests, specify conditions under which shipping could be permissible, evaluate large-scale testing for future safety improvements, and resolve the inconsistency between accepting the contract/delaying launches and your Not Ship recommendation.

criteria.C1: You identify the core ethical dilemma, link it to engineering design and competitive organisational context, and list stakeholders. To reach Excellent, develop the significance of several ethical issues and discuss each stakeholder’s interests, especially the chip contract company, whose interests are currently listed but not analysed.
criteria.C2: You provide structured for-and-against arguments and reach a clear decision. To reach Excellent, deepen the objective arguments and make decision-making recommendations for several different stakeholders, not only Rachel and the company; strengthen the pro-shipping case and show how trade-offs are weighed.
criteria.C3: Your logical structure supports the Not Ship conclusion, but the pro-shipping case is comparatively weak and the analysis is not systematic for all stakeholders. To reach Excellent, integrate a stakeholder-by-stakeholder analysis so each section builds the argument, and strengthen counterarguments before concluding.
criteria.C4: You use relevant qualitative evidence and external cases such as the NHS/HSSIB example. To reach Very good, substantiate arguments with adequate references and some qualitative/quantitative evidence; for Excellent, add balanced in-depth evidence. Correct the Volkswagen case to diesel emissions cheating, complete reference [3], fix [4], replace the hypothetical 1% with sourced risk data, and ensure the Apple reference directly supports your claim.
criteria.C5: Your report has a recognisable structure. To move up, add the required ~150-word abstract and at least one relevant table or figure, proofread for language accuracy, and format references consistently in Harvard or IEEE. Good requires limited visual elements and a few relevant references; Very good/Excellent require several visual types and extensive, relevant references.
